# On the Peculiar Art of Noticing

There's a quality to autumn light that makes me think about attention. The way it arrives at a lower angle than summer's direct assault from above, it seems to know how to illuminate details—the texture of a wall, the intricate veining of a leaf, the dust motes suspended in an otherwise invisible air. There's something generous about it, the way autumn light doesn't demand anything from you but does reward close looking.

I've been thinking lately about how much of life happens in the spaces between the things we're supposed to notice. Nobody's ever told you to pay attention to the exact sound a coffee cup makes when you set it down, yet there's a remarkable variety in those sounds depending on the cup's weight, the surface it meets, your frame of mind. A ceramic mug on a wooden table sounds entirely different from one on tile, and somehow that difference matters, even though we're trained from childhood to treat these moments as negligible background noise.

The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote that the aspects of things that are most important for us are hidden because of their simplicity and familiarity. It's a strange thought—that the things most important to us are hiding in plain sight, protected by their very ordinariness. We develop this habit of unseeking, where we learn to look past things in favor of whatever we've decided is significant. A child hasn't learned this habit yet, which is why they can spend forty-five minutes investigating an ant while you're waiting to go somewhere.

I wonder what we lose when we perfect this learned blindness, and what we might gain if we could partially unlearn it without losing the ability to function. There's probably a balance point—you can't notice everything; that way lies paralysis. But the culture we've built seems to encourage swinging almost entirely to the other extreme, where we're supposed to move efficiently through the world, eyes on the goal, filtering out ninety-nine percent of the sensory input available to us.

Technology has made this worse and better simultaneously. Worse because we're now trained to process information at increasing velocity, scrolling past images and ideas that might have once commanded our full attention. A photograph that would have been examined carefully for minutes in 1985 now gets a half-second of visual processing before we move on to the next one. But better in that we have tools that can magnify the invisible—microscopes that show us the architecture of a raindrop, time-lapse cameras that reveal the hidden motion in flowers blooming, recordings that let us hear frequencies outside human hearing range. Science has given us permission to notice things that aren't immediately obvious.

There's a Japanese word, *komorebi*, which refers specifically to the filtered sunlight that falls through the leaves of trees. The fact that this has its own word seems significant. It suggests that at some point, a culture of people decided that this particular phenomenon was worth naming, worth calling out as distinct from "sunlight" or "light through trees"—it deserved its own word because it deserved individual attention. I wonder how different our consciousness would be if we had specific words for all the small, precise things we currently lump together under generic categories.

I've been reading about the practice of forest bathing—*shinrin-yoku*—which is simply the act of walking slowly through a forest with no particular destination, allowing your senses to receive whatever they encounter. It's not about achievement or exercise. It's about presence, about letting the forest teach your senses what to notice. Studies show it reduces cortisol and increases parasympathetic nervous system activity, which is another way of saying it calms you down, but that description somehow misses the point. It's not primarily about stress reduction; that's just what happens when you stop filtering everything through the lens of utility and let yourself actually perceive.

The problem, of course, is that we're not all living in forests, and even those who are usually have somewhere to be. Modern life demands efficiency. And there's nothing wrong with efficiency; it's let us do remarkable things. But we've let efficiency colonize territories where it doesn't necessarily belong. We eat efficiently, which means we often don't taste our food. We commute efficiently, which means we don't notice the trees we pass every day or the changing light or the other people sharing the space with us. We work efficiently, which means we don't often take time to think deeply about anything.

Yet something in us resists this, too. There's been a renaissance of what we might call "slow practices"—slow food, slow fashion, slow reading. These practices are explicitly about returning attention to things that have been streamlined away. But there's something vaguely privileged about calling it a "practice," as though noticing things requires a particular discipline or class position. Which it shouldn't. Noticing should be free, available to everyone.

Maybe the real art is in finding moments where you don't have to choose between efficiency and attention. The commute that's also a time to notice the changing seasons. The meal eaten quickly but tasted carefully. The walk between one obligation and the next where you allow yourself to actually see the streets you're traveling through.

I think what draws me to autumn light is that it seems to make noticing easier. It's more forgiving somehow, more patient than summer's brightness. It has a quality of melancholy that matches the contemplative mood it encourages. Spring light is exciting, summer light is urgent, winter light is thin and searching. But autumn light seems to invite you to slow down and pay attention not because you should, but because there's something genuinely worth seeing if you do.

That might be the secret—finding or creating conditions where noticing becomes easier than not noticing. Where the friction is reversed. Where the path of least resistance leads toward attention rather than away from it.

The light is changing as I write this. That's the thing about paying attention to light—you get the bonus of watching it transform continuously. It's never the same twice. Every moment of genuine perception is unique, unrepeatable. Which makes noticing not just a pleasant activity but a form of gathering—collecting moments that will never come again.

Maybe that's enough reason to try.
